sentences.text: Boverisuchus is assumed to have had heavily armored skin and long limbs adapted for a running habitus. It possessed hoof-like toes, suggesting it lived primarily on land and likely hunted terrestrial mammals.
The animal had ziphodont teeth that were laterally compressed, sharp, and serrated, indicating it could not drown its prey.
Boverisuchus teeth were initially mistaken for theropod dinosaur teeth, leading to a false belief that non-avian dinosaurs survived the Cretaceous–Paleogene extinction.
Some specimens show a tail that was round in cross-section and lacked the osteoderm crest seen in modern crocodiles, resembling a dinosaur's tail.
The type species was originally described from Lutetian deposits in Germany alongside Weigeltisuchus geiseltalensis.
In 2026, Lindblad et al. described the first Boverisuchus specimen from the middle-late Paleocene of Saskatchewan, Canada.
Boverisuchus was reinstated as a valid genus in 2013 after Pristichampsus rollinati was deemed a nomen dubium due to insufficient diagnostic material.
The family name Planocraniidae was reinstated to include Boverisuchus and related genera, replacing the name Pristichampsidae.
Boverisuchus belongs to the family Planocraniidae, is classified within the order Crocodilia, and is classified within the suborder Eusuchia.
Boverisuchus fossils date from the Early to Middle Eocene, specifically the Ypresian to Lutetian stages.
The time range for Boverisuchus is estimated from 61.66 to 37.71 million years ago, spanning the Selandian to Bartonian stages.
Boverisuchus was a relatively small crocodyliform, estimated to reach 2.2 to 3.6 meters in length and weigh around 100 kilograms.
It is debated how to classify Planocraniidae, with a 2021 study noting a lack of consensus and difficulty in placing the group.
